results.claim: Every connected cograph other than a singleton or a graph with exactly one universal vertex is equivalent to the zero game.
results.proof_sketch: Let C be connected. Its cotree root is a join. If C has at least two universal vertices, pairing any two of them is a pairing dominating set, so C=0 by Remark 9. If C has no universal vertex, every root-join block has at least two vertices. Choose distinct a,b in one block and c,d in another. The disjoint pairs (a,b),(c,d) dominate C in the pairing sense: vertices in the first block lie in N[c]∩N[d], while all other vertices lie in N[a]∩N[b]. Hence C=0. The only remaining connected cases are K1 and components having a unique universal vertex.

results.claim: SHVG on cographs is polynomially equivalent to an explicit open-or-delete scoring game on rooted forests.
results.proof_sketch:
Construct a forest R(G) recursively over connected components. Ignore zero components from the preceding claim. A K1 component becomes a prize leaf. If a nontrivial component C has unique universal vertex u, make an internal root whose children are R(C-u).

Moves at u dominate other moves in C. For Maker, transpose u with any proposed first move x in a simulated strategy. If simulated u ultimately belongs to Maker, the final coloring is unchanged on {u,x}; if simulated u belongs to Breaker, the simulated contribution of C is zero while the transposed contribution is nonnegative. The analogous transposition proves dominance for Breaker.

Breaker claiming u makes C a zero position. After Maker claims u, the residual game is exactly C-u. Indeed, |C-u|≥2 and every nontrivial cograph contains twins a,b. Apply Theorem 13 both in C after u is Maker-owned and in C-u, virtually assigning a to Maker and b to Breaker. Vertex u is then spoiled by b, while every vertex of C-u is happy in C exactly when it is happy in C-u. These arguments remain valid after adjoining an arbitrary disjoint game, so they establish game equivalence. Thus Maker opening u exposes its child forest; Breaker taking u deletes its entire rooted tree. A prize leaf scores one only when Maker takes it.

Conversely, realize any rooted tree recursively: a prize leaf is K1; for an internal node, take the disjoint union of its child graphs and a zero K2 ballast, then join one new vertex to everything. That vertex is uniquely universal, the construction is a cograph, and a forest with L prize leaves and I internal nodes uses L+3I vertices and polynomially many edges. Therefore the two decision problems are polynomially interreducible.

results.claim: The cograph game is linear-time solvable when every tree in the reduced forest has outdegree at most two.
results.proof_sketch: There are only two relevant equivalence types. Let A denote a prize leaf and Z the zero game. Induct upward. A node whose children contain zero A-types has game {0|0}=Z. With one A-child, Maker opening it leaves Breaker to move on A, yielding zero; Breaker can delete it, so both starting scores are zero and Theorem 6 gives Z. With two A-children, their sum is the constant game 1: two prize leaves score one regardless of starter. Hence the parent has options “Maker obtains 1” and “Breaker obtains 0,” exactly the game A. Z-children may be omitted. Labeling nodes bottom-up therefore leaves z copies of A at the top. Their scores are ceil(z/2) for Maker-first and floor(z/2) for Breaker-first. Each cotree and forest node is processed once, giving linear time.

results.claim: Reduced forests of height one—equivalently, disjoint unions of stars and isolated vertices after zero components are removed—admit an O(n^2) exact algorithm.
results.proof_sketch:
Let k1≤⋯≤kr be the leaf counts of unopened stars and let l be the number of exposed prize leaves. Write M(i,l),B(i,l) for the values with stars k1,…,ki remaining. A simultaneous strong induction on the remaining nodes establishes monotonicity in exposed leaves and star size, together with the exchange inequality V_X(S∪{j},l+k)≥V_X(S∪{k},l+j) for j≤k and X∈{M,B}. Matching exposed-leaf moves, moves in other stars, and moves in the two distinguished stars proves the induction; opening the distinguished stars gives the same successor with l+j+k leaves. Thus Maker loses nothing by opening the largest remaining star, while Breaker minimizes by deleting it.

Consequently,
M(i,l)=max(1+B(i,l-1) if l>0, B(i-1,l+ki)),
B(i,l)=min(M(i,l-1) if l>0, M(i-1,l)).
The bases are M(0,l)=ceil(l/2), B(0,l)=floor(l/2), and unavailable leaf terms are omitted. Only states satisfying l+sum_{j≤i}kj≤K, where K is the total initial number of prize leaves, are needed. There are O(r(K+1)) such states, including the K=0 boundary case, so filling them after sorting costs O(n^2).

results.claim: The pair of standalone scores (Ms,Bs) is insufficient as a cotree dynamic-programming state.
results.proof_sketch: Both P3 and K1,3 have standalone scores (1,0). Nevertheless, P3+P3 has scores (1,1), whereas the height-one recurrence gives P3+K1,3 scores (2,1). Thus these components have identical left and right stops but different behavior in sums. Any full cotree algorithm must retain information richer than the two starting-player scores.

final_writeup:
A complete complexity classification is not obtained, but the remaining problem has an exact, substantially simpler form.

Given a cograph G, discard every connected component having either no universal vertex or at least two universal vertices: each has an explicit pairing dominating set and is therefore the zero game. Recursively replace every remaining nontrivial component C, with unique universal vertex u, by a rooted tree whose root represents u and whose children represent C-u. Singletons become prize leaves.

The resulting open-or-delete forest game is exact. On Maker's turn, choosing an internal root removes it and exposes its children; choosing a prize leaf removes it and scores one. On Breaker's turn, choosing any root deletes its entire rooted subtree. For a forest F, its unrestricted exact recurrence is

M(F)=max_T {1+B(F-T) if T is a prize leaf; B(F-T+children(T)) otherwise},
B(F)=min_T M(F-T).

The forward forest has at most one node per retained graph vertex. Conversely, a forest with L prize leaves and I internal nodes becomes a cograph with L+3I vertices and polynomially many edges. Starting player, score, and threshold are preserved, so classifying SHVG on cographs is polynomially equivalent to classifying this rooted-forest game. This formulation also explains why the neighborhood-diversity algorithm does not immediately become polynomial: distinct rooted projects interact through the global alternation of moves.

Two genuine polynomial subcases follow. If every reduced tree has outdegree at most two, every subtree collapses bottom-up to either zero or one prize-leaf game, giving a linear algorithm. If the reduced forest has height one, it is a collection of stars and exposed leaves; sorting star sizes and applying the displayed two-parameter recurrence gives an O(n^2) algorithm for both possible starters.

The unrestricted rooted-forest game remains unresolved here. No polynomial-time algorithm or matching hardness theorem is established for arbitrary reduced forests. In particular, merely storing (Ms,Bs) at cotree nodes cannot work: P3 and K1,3 both have (1,0), but their sums with P3 have different values. Thus the result is a precise reduction and two nontrivial tractable frontiers, rather than the requested full classification.
